editor_spans.body: Calling the Derby headquarters a step towards public control hides how slow the change is. Construction at Becketwell is not due to begin until early 2027 or finish until spring 2029. That is close to the latest date for the next general election, so the building that is meant to stand for the change will barely be ready before voters judge the government.

The benefits the government lists come from separate causes. A fare freeze is something ministers decided to pay for. It is not something public ownership produces by itself, and the next freeze will be a decision about spending, not about who runs the railway. The new trains depend on the £1 billion contract at Alstom's Derby site, which would have kept that factory busy under any ownership model.

The size of the jobs promise matters. The building will hold up to 450 staff, many of whom are likely to move from existing rail organisations rather than fill new posts. The 600 apprenticeships are spread over four years, and the industry says fewer than 7% of its workers are under 25. That is a symbolic answer to an ageing workforce, not an answer in proportion to the problem. The bigger story is Derby: the government is using it, like its other regional announcements, to show it is moving power and money out of London.

Taken over five days, the government's Ukraine statements show a policy pulled two ways. On 9 October the government said it 'fully supports US-led efforts' and pointed to energy prices and the cost of living. On 12 October the Prime Minister said the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets was an energy ceasefire. He welcomed President Trump's reciprocal ceasefire before any start date had been set. By 14 October Downing Street was describing Russia's 'blatant' attacks since that call. The British interest is clear: lower fuel prices at home without seeming to reward Moscow. But it made London rely on a US-designed truce that Russia has ignored.

The headline of 'doubling down' promises more than the money does. The new air defence package is £45 million. Only £10 million of it is being sped up for winter, against an existing £1.6 billion commitment for missiles. The larger sanctions, military and financial packages have so far only been requested from ministers. Meanwhile Britain is asking partners to copy its ban on shipping services for Russian LNG. That pushes the same energy squeeze Britain says it wants eased for diesel. It is coherent only if the ceasefire actually happens.

The Prime Minister's 'offer' to Holyrood is really a challenge. Local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster has no power to hand Scottish regions anything. It can only shame the Scottish Government by calling it one of the most centralised in Europe. Andy Burnham is offering the city-region model that made his name in Manchester, delivered through No10 North and the Scotland Office. In effect it creates a second route by which Westminster can deal directly with Scottish regions. The Derby headquarters and the East Midlands mayor's comments come from the same playbook. Whether Scotland's First Minister accepts will show whether this is about governing or about positioning.

The Crown's new representative in Tyrone has a biography the notice states without comment. He was the police District Commander in Omagh on the day of the 1998 bombing, and the conduct of police and intelligence agencies before the bombing is still disputed. Appointing a long-serving former RUC officer and Presbyterian elder in a county with a nationalist majority follows the usual pattern for lieutenancy appointments. It also shows how slowly the ceremonial institutions of Northern Ireland have changed compared with the political ones.
